hypotheses.text: Behavioral dysregulation (HP:0000708) in FBXO11-related neurodevelopmental disorder is an incompletely penetrant feature (~60-85% across independent cohorts) rather than an obligatory diagnostic criterion, meaning that the absence of overt hyperactivity or aggression cannot rule out FBXO11 variants, particularly in familial or milder presentations.
hypotheses.rationale: Initial cohorts such as Gregor et al. (2018) reported behavioral problems in 85% (17/20), whereas larger follow-up series such as Goel et al. (2026) observed behavioral dysregulation in only 62% (13/21), and familial reports describe predominantly mild intellectual disability with variable or muted behavioral phenotypes. Testing whether behavioral disruption is non-obligatory prevents clinicians from missing quiet or mildly affected individuals.

evidence.text: In a cohort of 20 individuals with de novo FBXO11 variants, behavioral problems including autistic features were documented in 17 of 20 (85%) individuals.

hypotheses.text: The simultaneous presence of axial/congenital hypotonia (HP:0001252) alongside disruptive behavioral disturbances (HP:0000708) is a distinctive signature of FBXO11-related disorder that differentiates it from non-syndromic ADHD or purely hyperactive neurobehavioral conditions.
hypotheses.rationale: While disruptive behaviors (ADHD, aggression, autistic traits) are common in many neuropsychiatric presentations, FBXO11 patients concurrently exhibit early neuromuscular findings, notably hypotonia and joint hyperlaxity, in over 60% of cases (e.g. 62% in Goel et al. 2026; Jansen et al. 2019), offering an objective neuromotor discriminator.

evidence.text: Hypotonia is identified as one of the most prevalent systemic findings in FBXO11-related NDD, occurring in 62% of affected individuals alongside behavioural dysregulation (62%).

source.quote: All individuals had borderline to severe ID and behavioral problems (autism spectrum disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, anxiety, aggression) were observed in most of them. The most relevant common facial features included a thin upper lip and a broad prominent space between the paramedian peaks of the upper lip. Other features were hypotonia and hyperlaxity of the joints.

hypotheses.text: The neurobehavioral phenotype in FBXO11 deficiency exhibits longitudinal age-dependent evolution, transitioning from childhood hyperactive/aggressive dysregulation (ADHD, temper tantrums) to adolescent and adult internalizing psychiatric symptoms such as anxiety and depression.
hypotheses.rationale: Apparent discrepancies in behavioral penetrance between cohorts may stem from cross-sectional evaluations at different ages. Longitudinal observations in familial and adolescent patients (such as Lee et al. 2020) demonstrate childhood ADHD evolving with depressive/affective disorders, explaining why adult carriers may lack overt externalizing hyperactivity.

evidence.text: Case documentation indicates ADHD and depression evaluated and managed sequentially from childhood through early adolescence and adulthood in a patient with a confirmed FBXO11 frameshift variant.

new_directions.question_text: Does the prevalence and severity of disruptive externalizing behaviors correlate with variant class (truncating/loss-of-function versus domain-specific missense variants) or inheritance mode (de novo vs familial transmission) in FBXO11?
new_directions.rationale: Ascertainment bias via de novo exome trios often selects for severe neurobehavioral manifestations, whereas familial inherited cases and certain missense variants may manifest with attenuated neurodevelopmental profiles.

new_directions.question_text: What is the systematic performance of combining craniofacial gestalt metrics with behavioral screening compared to behavioral screening alone in discriminating FBXO11 from overlapping ID syndromes?
new_directions.rationale: Recent computational phenotyping (e.g., GestaltMatcher in Goel et al. 2026) detected measurable facial similarity across FBXO11 individuals; evaluating its discrimination power when combined with neurobehavioral assessments would resolve whether behavioral variability impairs clinical diagnosis.
